reels.title: Three Afterlives
reels.hook: Three afterlives. You only get one

beats.text: Egypt. Your heart weighed against Maat's feather. Spell 125.
Too heavy. Ammit devours it. Crocodile, lion, hippopotamus.
The North. Odin takes half the slain. Freyja the rest. Grimnismal.
Tibet. Forty-nine days in the bardo. Bardo Thodol read aloud.
Which would you risk? Comment one, two or three.

reels.caption:
Three afterlives. Three different tests.
In Egypt, Spell 125 of the Book of the Dead weighs the heart against the feather of Maat.
In the Grimnismal, Odin and Freyja divide the battle-slain.
In Tibet, the Bardo Thodol is read to the dead across forty-nine days between lives.
Each judges something different.
Choose one. Comment 1, 2 or 3 below.
Every road past death: alloccult.com/death-afterlife/afterlife-cosmologies

review_log.summary: All beats are accurate. Spell 125 and the heart against Maat's feather are correct. Ammit is a crocodile, lion and hippopotamus composite. Grímnismál 14 divides the slain between Freyja and Odin. The Bardo Thödol is read over the 49-day intermediate state. The Yama painting is clearly related to Tibetan death and bardo judgement imagery, and the memento mori etching fits the closing call to action. Text is legible and short, the hook works, and the caption is accurate. Nothing blocking.

reels.title: The Six-Month Operation
reels.hook: Six months of prayer. Then the demons

beats.text: The Book of Abramelin. Attributed to Abraham of Worms. Dated 1458.
1898: Mathers translates a French copy. Bibliotheque de l'Arsenal, Paris.
His copy demands six months of withdrawal. German copies: eighteen.
The reward: your Holy Guardian Angel. Then the spirits are bound.
1899: Crowley buys Boleskine House to begin. He leaves it unfinished.

reels.caption:
The Book of Abramelin claims to date from 1458.
S. L. MacGregor Mathers translated a French copy in 1898, from the Bibliotheque de l'Arsenal in Paris.
It prescribes six months of prayer and withdrawal.
German manuscripts, edited later, demand eighteen.
Then the angel. Then the spirits.
In 1899 Crowley bought Boleskine House to attempt it.
By 1900 he had left for Paris.
The full manuscript tradition: alloccult.com/grimoires-sacred-texts/classical-grimoires

review_log.summary: Facts check out. The six-month French version used by Mathers, the eighteen-month German manuscripts, the 1458 self-date, Crowley buying Boleskine in 1899 and abandoning the working in 1900 are all accurate. The reel correctly departs from the archive page, which reverses the six- and eighteen-month figures. Mathers's edition was published in 1898, so departing from the archive's 1897 is justified. Images are relevant and legible, and the hook works. Only polish remains: 'Dated 1458' could read as a scholarly date, the missing accent in Bibliothèque, and the caption's vague 'By 1900'.

reels.title: The Planet That Rules Your Birthday
reels.hook: The day you were born has a ruler

beats.text: Seven wandering lights. Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon.
Each ruled one hour in turn. The first hour named the day. Cassius Dio recorded it.
Saturday, Saturn. Sunday, the Sun. Monday, the Moon.
Tuesday, Mars: Tiw, mardi. Wednesday, Mercury: Woden, mercredi.
Thursday, Jupiter: Thor, jeudi. Friday, Venus: Frigg, vendredi. Comment your day.

reels.caption:
The seven-day week is a planetary clock.
Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon: each ruled an hour, in that order.
The planet of the first hour named the day.
Cassius Dio set it down in the third century.
English kept the Norse gods. French kept the Roman ones.
Comment the day you were born — we'll answer with your ruler. Save this. ☉
The full system: alloccult.com/divination-arts/astrology

review_log.summary: Accurate, well-built reel. The Chaldean order, the hour-ruler mechanism, Cassius Dio (Roman History 37.18–19) and the weekday etymologies all check out. Nothing blocking. Polish only: slide 3 runs slightly long, slide 6's Gigantomachy image shows Jupiter only faintly, and the caption calls the English weekday gods 'Norse' (they are Anglo-Saxon/Germanic) and carries a ☉ symbol against the no-emoji rule.

reels.title: Directions for the Dead
reels.hook: The dead were buried with directions

beats.text: Petelia, southern Italy. Fourth century BC. A sheet of gold, folded small.
To the left of the house of Hades, a spring. A white cypress.
Do not drink there. Find the cold water of Memory.
Guardians stand before it. The tablet gives the words to say.
"I am a child of Earth and starry Heaven." The password.

reels.caption:
Found at Petelia, southern Italy. Fourth century BC.
A gold tablet, folded, buried with the dead.
It warns of a spring beside a white cypress — do not drink there.
Seek the cold water flowing from the Lake of Memory.
Tell its guardians: "I am a child of Earth and starry Heaven."
The tablet is now in the British Museum.
Read the rest of the instructions: alloccult.com/ancient-mystery-schools/orphic-mysteries

review_log.summary: Accurate, on-brand reel on the Petelia gold tablet (4th c. BC, southern Italy, now in the British Museum). The quoted lines match the tablet text and the archive page. The hook is strong and every slide is legible. The images are relevant: a Boitard underworld etching with Charon, and Grignion's 1789 Pluto/Hades with Cerberus. There are only minor polish notes, and nothing blocks posting.

reels.title: The Hierarchy · I: The First Triad
reels.hook: Nine choirs. You were only shown the last

beats.text: c. 500 AD. A writer signs as Dionysius the Areopagite, Paul's convert.
The Celestial Hierarchy. Nine choirs. Three triads.
Seraphim. Six wings. Two veil the face, two the feet. Isaiah 6:2.
Cherubim. Four faces: man, lion, ox, eagle. Ezekiel 1:10.
Thrones, bound to Ezekiel's wheels. Rims full of eyes. Hierarchy II: next Friday.

reels.caption:
Hierarchy I.
Around 500 AD, a writer took the name of Dionysius the Areopagite — the Athenian Paul converts in Acts 17:34.
His Celestial Hierarchy ordered heaven into nine choirs.
First triad: Seraphim, Cherubim, Thrones.
Isaiah saw six wings. Ezekiel saw four faces, and wheels with rims full of eyes.
Hierarchy II next Friday: the middle triad.
Save the series: alloccult.com/ceremonial-magic/angelology

review_log.summary: Facts check out: Pseudo-Dionysius c. 500, nine choirs in three triads, Isaiah 6:2, Ezekiel 1:10, rims full of eyes (Ezekiel 1:18), Acts 17:34. Images fit their beats, are period engravings, and are legible. Only polish notes remain: the hook lacks a final period, and Ezekiel 1 calls the creatures 'living creatures', naming them cherubim only at 10:20.

reels.title: Sixty-Nine Hours on a Snakeskin
reels.hook: She lay three days on a snakeskin

beats.text: New Orleans, late 1920s. Zora Neale Hurston, a student of Franz Boas.
She sought the hoodoo doctors. Luke Turner claimed Marie Laveau as kin.
Initiation: face down, navel to a snakeskin. Sixty-nine hours. No food.
She rose with a new name: the Rain-Bringer.
1935. She put it in print: Mules and Men.

reels.caption:
Zora Neale Hurston studied under Franz Boas.
In late-1920s New Orleans, she went looking for hoodoo doctors.
Luke Turner claimed Marie Laveau as his kin.
Her initiation: sixty-nine hours face down, her navel touching a snakeskin, without food.
She came out with a name: the Rain-Bringer.
She published it all in Mules and Men, 1935.
The full tradition: alloccult.com/witchcraft-folk-magic/hoodoo-rootwork

review_log.summary: Facts match Hurston's own account in Mules and Men (1935). She studied under Boas and did New Orleans fieldwork in 1928–29. Luke Turner claimed to be Marie Laveau's nephew. Her initiation was sixty-nine hours face down, navel to a snakeskin, without food, and she was named the Rain-Bringer. The hook's 'three days' rounds the sixty-nine hours and echoes Hurston's own framing. All slides are legible and well under the length limit, and the hook stops a scroll. Caption and hashtags are on brand. Nothing blocking.

reels.title: The Card Test
reels.hook: Name this card before it turns

beats.text: Duke University, 1934. J. B. Rhine publishes Extra-Sensory Perception.
Five symbols, designed by Karl Zener. Circle, cross, waves, square, star.
Twenty-five cards. Chance alone gives you five correct.
Hubert Pearce guessed from another building. Rhine reported about thirty percent.
Critics found the controls weak. The card turns. Did you call it?

reels.caption:
In 1934, J. B. Rhine of Duke University published Extra-Sensory Perception.
His test used five symbols, designed by Karl Zener.
Twenty-five cards. Chance predicts five hits.
Hubert Pearce, a divinity student, guessed from another building.
Rhine reported about thirty percent.
Critics found the controls weak.
Comment your guess before you rewatch. ☽
The full record: alloccult.com/consciousness/psychic-abilities

review_log.summary: Facts check out. Rhine published Extra-Sensory Perception in 1934. Karl Zener designed the five symbols. Chance expectation is 5 of 25. Pearce, a divinity student, guessed from the Duke library in the Pearce-Pratt series at roughly 30%. Critics did attack the controls. Nothing blocking remains. Polish notes: segment 4 should say chance 'predicts' rather than 'gives'. The caption's crescent-moon glyph should go under the no-emoji rule. The segment 5 engraving is a 19th-century mind-reading act, not Duke, but it is thematically related and credited, so it is acceptable.
